records.our_prose: The three numbers on a fertilizer bag are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (N-P-K). Beets do well with a balanced blend where the numbers are about even, like a 10-10-10, mixed into the soil before planting along with some compost. Do not pile on high-nitrogen fertilizer, which gives you lots of leaves and small roots. The one extra thing beets care about is boron, and only add that if a soil test says to.

records.our_prose: Beets give you two harvests. You can pick the leaves young all along, taking a few outer ones per plant so the root keeps growing, and the seedlings you thin out are your first baby greens. The roots are ready by size, not a set date: brush the soil off a shoulder and pull when the beet is about 1 1/2 to 2 inches across, the sweet, tender stage, usually around 50 to 70 days. You can let them grow up to about 3 inches, but bigger beets get woody and strong. There is no rush in cool weather: they get sweeter after a light frost and hold in the ground, and the roots take more cold than the leaves. In cold areas, pile straw over the row and dig them into early winter until the ground freezes. Pull by hand, or loosen with a fork in heavy soil, and twist off the tops, leaving an inch of stem on beets you want to store so they do not bleed out their color.

records.our_prose: St. George's Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) grows beets on two direct-sown cycles, per Utah State University Extension's suggested vegetable planting dates for Utah. The spring sowing runs March 1 to March 15, the Group B (Semi-Hardy) date for St. George, with roots ready in about 58 days and the crop pulled by mid-May before the heat builds. USU Extension's Washington County frost and elevation notes put St. George over 100°F in June, July, and August; since the documented fall window (USU's Group E "Special Plants for Fall Harvest" table) does not open until July 1, June is a genuine bare-ground pause between the two cycles. The fall sowing runs July 1 to August 1, and USU's fall-gardening guidance for the St. George area specifically groups beets with turnips and carrots as roots that hold well and can be dug quite late into winter, well past the November 1 average first frost.

records.our_prose: Direct-sow beets into the garden; they resent transplanting and are simplest grown from seed in place. Sow about 1/2 inch deep once the soil is workable and at least 45 to 50°F, roughly 2 to 3 weeks before the last spring frost, and again in late summer for a fall crop. Soaking the seed in warm water for about 24 hours before sowing speeds the slow germination. The key beet-specific point is that each beet seed is a multigerm seedball, a dried fruit containing several embryos, so a single seed sprouts a small cluster of seedlings and the stand must be thinned. Monogerm cultivars (one seedling per seed) avoid this. Keep the surface moist and uncrusted until the seedlings emerge, often 1 to 2 weeks.

records.our_prose: For larger harvests, beets are good keepers. In cold climates they can be left in the ground under a thick straw mulch and pulled until the soil freezes hard, or packed unwashed in damp sand or sawdust in a box in a root cellar or unheated garage held near 32 to 40°F at high humidity, where they hold for two to four months. Store roots only; use the greens fresh.

records.our_prose: For larger harvests, beets are good keepers. In cold climates they can be left in the ground under a thick straw mulch and pulled until the soil freezes hard, or packed unwashed in damp sand or sawdust in a box in a root cellar or unheated garage held near 32 to 40°F at high humidity, where they hold for two to four months. Store roots only; use the greens fresh.

records.source_context: However, beet roots can be harvested anytime after the root reaches 1 inch in diameter. Beets will tolerate temperatures down to about 20ºF, so they can be left in the garden late into the fall. Twist off the leaves rather than cutting them to prevent “bleeding” which causes less intense color and perhaps less flavor.

records.our_prose: Even, consistent moisture is the rule, and it matters most during the slow germination window and again as the roots size up. From sowing until the seedlings are up, often 1 to 2 weeks, the surface must stay moist and uncrusted. Once established, beets want steady moisture rather than a wet-dry swing: aim for about 1 inch of water per week including rain, delivered in deeper, less frequent soakings.

records.source_context: Care for the herb garden is the same as for a vegetable or flower garden. Watering Water as necessary during dry periods. Generally, herbs need about 1 inch of water per week, either from rainfall or from irrigation. Mulch will help conserve soil moisture as well as reduce weed growth.

records.our_prose: Beets do not regrow a new root after you pull them, since each plant makes one root. A planting is ready about 50 to 70 days after sowing and you harvest it over a couple of weeks, while the leaves give a longer, light harvest. For a steady supply, plant a new short row every 2 to 3 weeks.

records.source_context: Keep the cultivation shallow to avoid root injury. Harvest & Storage: Harvest beets about 50 to 70 days after planting. Beets should be harvested at 1½ to 2 inches in diameter. Beets allowed to get larger than 2 inches in diameter may be woody.
